c.tagline: Brick-Gothic 'Queen of the Hanseatic League', marzipan, and Baltic charm.

taxi.fareNote: Cream taxis are metered and regulated; find them at ranks by the Hauptbahnhof and squares or book via Free Now or by phone. A ride across town runs roughly 10-15 EUR.

emergency.note: 112 reaches ambulance and fire across the EU; 110 is the direct police line. Both are free from any phone.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The area around the Hauptbahnhof can be scruffy late at night; otherwise usual city awareness.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed old-town island ringed by the Trave, home to the twin-towered Holstentor, the medieval Rathaus, seven church towers, the Niederegger marzipan house, and the Buddenbrookhaus of Thomas Mann; best for first-timers who want every landmark within a walkable core.

The lively mainland district just west of the old town around the Hauptbahnhof and the ZOB bus station, with hotels, shops, and everyday restaurants; the most convenient base for arriving by train or bus.

A leafy, well-to-do residential quarter northeast of the island along the Wakenitz river, with the wooden-boat Museumshafen, parks, and quiet villa streets; suits travellers after calm, greenery, and waterside walks.

A relaxed southern residential area home to the University of Lübeck and its medical campus, with student cafes, sports grounds, and easy access to the old town; good for longer stays and a local, low-key feel.

Lübeck's Baltic seaside borough at the mouth of the Trave, with a wide sandy beach, promenade, casino, lighthouse, and the Skandinavienkai ferry port to Scandinavia; the go-to for beach days and sea air, about 20 km from the centre.

water.note: Tap water is safe and strictly regulated, as everywhere in Germany.

transit.pay: Buy tickets in the app, from machines, or the driver (cards accepted); a single fare is about €2.90 and the Deutschland-Ticket (€63/month) covers all local transit nationwide.
transit.hours: Stadtverkehr Lübeck buses run roughly 4:30am to around midnight, with night buses on weekends; the compact old-town island is easily walked.
transit.note: Lübeck has no U-Bahn or tram - Stadtverkehr Lübeck buses are the backbone, while the walled old-town island is best explored on foot or by bike; regional trains reach Travemünde and the Baltic coast.

ferry: Skandinavienkai, Travemünde (ferries to Scandinavia & the Baltic)

transit.m: S-Bahn S1 to Hamburg Hbf, then DB regional train to Lübeck Hbf (~75-90 min total)
Taxi from Hamburg Airport to Lübeck (50-60 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good service is customary. Tell the server the total you want to pay as you hand over the money.

food.name: Lubecker Marzipan
food.desc: The city's protected almond confection, softer and less sugary than most. Sold as loaves, fruit shapes and bars, and folded into cakes and tortes.

places.name: Cafe Niederegger
places.note: Marzipan house since 1806, with a cafe, huge shop and a free marzipan museum upstairs.

places.name: Marzipan-Speicher
places.note: Smaller local maker for comparing styles away from the Niederegger crowds.

places.name: Markt stalls
places.note: Seasonal market stands selling marzipan alongside baked goods in front of the Rathaus.

food.name: Fischbrotchen
food.desc: A crusty roll packed with Baltic fish: pickled herring, matjes or fried fillet, plus onion, pickle and remoulade. The perfect harbourside snack.

places.name: Untertrave harbour kiosks
places.note: Fish stands and boats along the river quay; the classic spot to eat one standing up.

places.name: Travemunde Vorderreihe kiosks
places.note: Seafront row at the Baltic beach resort, 20 minutes out by train, with the freshest catch.

places.name: Lubeck Wochenmarkt
places.note: Market fishmongers make them to order on market mornings.

food.name: Labskaus
food.desc: A sailor's plate of mashed corned beef, potato and beetroot, crowned with a fried egg and flanked by rollmops and gherkins. Looks alarming, tastes brilliant.

places.name: Schiffergesellschaft
places.note: Seafarers' guild house from 1535 with ship models and long benches; the definitive setting.

places.name: Ratskeller zu Lubeck
places.note: Vaulted cellar under the town hall serving north German classics.

places.name: Kartoffelkeller
places.note: Potato-focused cellar restaurant doing hearty regional plates at fair prices.

food.name: Rote Grutze
food.desc: Northern Germany's summer dessert: red berries and cherries cooked into a glossy compote and served cold under a flood of vanilla sauce or cream.

places.name: Cafe Niederegger
places.note: Cafe upstairs pairs it with marzipan cakes and proper filter coffee.

places.name: Schiffergesellschaft
places.note: Traditional finish to a heavy north German meal in a historic hall.

places.name: Ratskeller zu Lubeck
places.note: Reliable classic version with vanilla sauce.

food.name: Berliner
food.desc: A sugared, deep-fried yeast doughnut filled with jam, eaten with morning coffee across the north. Best while still slightly warm from the fryer.

places.name: Baeckerei Junge
places.note: Lubeck-founded bakery chain from 1897 with branches all over the old town.

places.name: Lubeck Wochenmarkt
places.note: Bakery stalls on market days, often with seasonal fillings.

places.name: Cafe Niederegger
places.note: Pastry counter for a sit-down version with cake alternatives.

food.name: Grunkohl
food.desc: Winter kale stewed slowly with smoked sausage, bacon and caramelised potatoes. A Schleswig-Holstein ritual served from the first frost through to spring.

places.name: Schiffergesellschaft
places.note: Serves it in season with Kochwurst and Kassler in a 16th-century dining hall.

places.name: Kartoffelkeller
places.note: Cosy cellar with big winter portions and roast potatoes on the side.

places.name: Ratskeller zu Lubeck
places.note: Traditional town hall cellar with a seasonal regional menu.

food.name: Rotspon
food.desc: Lubeck's own oddity: French red wine shipped north in barrel and matured in the city's cellars since Hanseatic times, said to soften on the journey.

places.name: Carl Tesdorpf
places.note: Wine merchant trading in Lubeck since 1678; the historic home of Rotspon.

places.name: Schiffergesellschaft
places.note: Pours it by the glass with dinner, exactly as merchants once drank it.

places.name: Ratskeller zu Lubeck
places.note: Town hall cellar with a wine list leaning on local Rotspon bottlings.

food.name: Brauberger unfiltered beer
food.desc: Cloudy, unfiltered Zwickelbier brewed in the old town to a recipe that predates the copper kettles it comes from. Fresh, malty and only available on site.

places.name: Brauberger zu Lubeck
places.note: Working brewpub with vaulted rooms; the beer never leaves the building unfiltered.

places.name: Kartoffelkeller
places.note: Good regional beer list to go with heavy northern food.

places.name: Untertrave riverside bars
places.note: Terraces facing the Trave for a beer with a view of the salt warehouses.

landmarks: Holstentor (Holsten Gate)
The twin-towered 1478 brick gate, leaning charmingly under its own weight, is Germany's most famous city gate and the enduring emblem of Hanseatic Lübeck.
St. Mary's Church (Marienkirche)
The mother church of Brick Gothic raised the world's highest brick vault, and its shattered bells, left where they fell in 1942, remain a haunting war memorial.
Lübeck Old Town (Altstadt Island)
Ringed by water, the UNESCO-listed medieval core bristles with seven spires, gabled merchant houses, and hidden courtyard passages called Gänge.
European Hansemuseum
This state-of-the-art museum at the old town's northern tip immerses visitors in the rise and fall of the Hanseatic League's medieval trading empire.
Niederegger Marzipan Café and Museum
The world's most famous marzipan house has sweetened Breite Strasse since 1806; its upstairs salon displays life-size marzipan figures above heavenly nut-cake.
Buddenbrookhaus
The gabled white townhouse immortalized in Thomas Mann's Nobel-winning novel 'Buddenbrooks' commemorates Lübeck's great literary family, the Manns.
St. Peter's Church Tower (St. Petri)
An elevator whisks visitors up this deconsecrated Gothic church's tower for the definitive panorama of Lübeck's spires, gables, and encircling waterways.
Heiligen-Geist-Hospital (Hospital of the Holy Spirit)
One of the world's oldest social institutions, founded in 1286, opens its frescoed chapel and rows of tiny almshouse cabins to visitors.
Salzspeicher (Salt Storehouses)
Six gabled brick warehouses beside the Holstentor once stored Lüneburg salt bound for the Baltic, and famously starred in the 1922 vampire film 'Nosferatu.'
Lübeck Cathedral (Dom)
Founded by Henry the Lion in 1173, the twin-spired cathedral houses Bernt Notke's monumental 17-meter triumphal cross above its serene whitewashed nave.

train.note: Lubeck Hauptbahnhof is a short walk west of the Altstadt island. Services are regional and IC rather than high-speed: Hamburg is about 45 minutes and runs twice an hour, Hamburg Airport is direct, and other trains serve Kiel, Puttgarden and Szczecin-bound regional lines. No train crosses the border here - since the Puttgarden-Rodby train ferry ended in December 2019, Copenhagen trains run out of Hamburg via Flensburg and Jutland instead, so you backtrack to Hamburg rather than heading north. A local line continues from the Hauptbahnhof out to Travemunde, calling at Lubeck-Travemunde Skandinavienkai for the Baltic ferries and Travemunde Strand for the beach.

bus.note: No scheduled international coach starts in Lubeck. FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) serves the ZOB beside the Hauptbahnhof on domestic runs to Hamburg, Berlin and the Baltic coast, and Scandinavian services are joined in Hamburg, 45 minutes away by train. Regional buses run by Stadtverkehr Lubeck and the NAH.SH network cover Travemunde, Timmendorfer Strand and the surrounding Holstein villages. Tickets are cheapest online.

intl.to: Trelleborg & Karlshamn (Sweden) - from the Skandinavienkai terminal in Travemunde
Klaipeda (Lithuania) - from the Skandinavienkai terminal in Travemunde
Malmo (Sweden) & Helsinki (Finland) - from the Skandinavienkai terminal in Travemunde
Liepaja (Latvia) - from the Skandinavienkai terminal in Travemunde

ferry.note: Travemunde is Germany's biggest Baltic ferry port and is part of Lubeck, about 20 km north-east and reached in around 20 minutes by regional train to Lubeck-Travemunde Skandinavienkai, which sits at the terminal itself. Crossings are long: Trelleborg is roughly 7-9 hours, Malmo about 9 hours, Klaipeda around 20 hours, Liepaja some 27 hours and Helsinki close to 30 hours, so most sailings are overnight and a cabin is worth booking. These are working Ro-Ro freight ships that also carry passengers rather than cruise ferries, so expect a functional rather than luxurious experience. Vehicle space must be reserved well in advance for summer sailings, and foot passengers should allow extra time as the terminal is laid out for cars and lorries.

half.name: Hamburg
half.blurb: Germany's second-largest city about 45 minutes from Lübeck by train, with the Speicherstadt warehouse district and Elbphilharmonie concert hall on the harbor.

half.name: Kiel
half.blurb: A Baltic port city an hour from Lübeck, home to a major sailing harbor and the annual Kiel Week regatta each summer.

half.name: Ratzeburg
half.blurb: A small island town on a lake south of Lübeck with a Romanesque brick cathedral founded by Henry the Lion in the 12th century.

half.name: Wismar
half.blurb: A Hanseatic port town on the Baltic coast east of Lübeck with a UNESCO-listed old town of brick gabled merchant houses.
